# Public interoperability fixtures

Every identifier, key, nonce, passphrase, body and token in these fixtures is
fictional public test data. Fixed nonces must never be used by the application.
Fixtures are checked in so normal Cargo verification needs no Python or Swift
installation and no network service.

`backup-v1.json` is generated by [`../reference/backup.py`](../reference/backup.py)
with Python's standard library and the installed OpenSSL EVP implementation.
It follows `snippets/Core/EncryptedSnippetBackup.swift`: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with
NFC input, the exact length-framed payload AAD, HKDF vault-key wrapping and padded
AES-256-GCM envelopes. It contains both halves of a fictional library, future
metadata and a device-local receipt which the portable decoder must remove.
Cargo reads only the checked-in JSON. The same development-only script's
`--verify` mode independently opens a Rust-generated public backup, then checks
the recovered vault key, record bodies and keyed hashes. Production exports use
600,000 KDF iterations and fresh random keys/identities/nonces; lower costs occur
only in internal test calls. Live execution between the native Apple and Linux
applications remains unverified.

`pam-module.c` is a public fictional Linux-PAM module. Native owner tests compile
it and a disposable helper, and load it only through `pam_start_confdir` with a
temporary policy. It uses a fictional password and never reads authentication
databases, keyrings or host policy. Cases include denied credentials, account
expiry/password-change requirements, changed identity, cached success without a
password prompt, unsupported or repeated prompts, and a stalled module.
The fixture directory is compiled into that disposable helper through
`SNIP_OWNER_FIXTURE_MAIN`; Cargo never enables this entry point. The installed
helper uses only the fixed system `system-auth` service, with no configurable
service, alternate policy directory or environment selector. Tests require the
same C compiler and PAM headers used to build the native application.

`loopback-ca.der`, `loopback-server.der` and `loopback-public-test-key.der` are
public fictional TLS fixtures generated with OpenSSL 3.6.4 by
[`../reference/tls-fixture.sh`](../reference/tls-fixture.sh). The server certificate
covers `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, has a ten-year validity period, and chains to
the fixture CA. The PKCS#8 private key is public test data, not application key
material. Rustls serves a disposable loopback server; the test client trusts only
this fixture CA with certificate verification enabled. An ordinary client test
rejects that certificate. No application trust configuration or host certificate
store is changed. Regenerate the fixtures if their validity expires; normal Cargo
tests consume their checked-in bytes and do not need OpenSSL.

`crypto-v1.json` was generated independently with Python cryptography 50.0.1,
backed by OpenSSL. It exercises the Swift schema-1 vault, its record HKDF and AAD,
ISO-7816 padding, HMAC plaintext digest, PBKDF2 passphrase wrap and recovery wrap.
The generator was a development tool; Python is not an app dependency.

`bootstrap-v1.json` is independently generated by
[`../reference/bootstrap.py`](../reference/bootstrap.py), using Python
cryptography 50.0.1 and OpenSSL. It covers P-256 ECDH pairing envelopes, invitation
AAD and comparison codes, recovery codes and AES-GCM envelopes, deterministic
Ed25519 library authority, signed challenges and exact request-body hashes.
The recovery ciphertext, authority public key and signature also match the
fixed examples in the existing Swift and Android bootstrap tests. Regenerating
this fixture is a development task; Cargo consumes the checked-in JSON directly.

`swift-double-v1.tsv` contains 11,903 binary64 bit patterns and their exact Swift
decimal spelling, generated by the upstream Swift 6.2 runtime's C99 formatter.
The corpus includes zero/sign, subnormal limits, maximum finite double, the 2^53
format transition, adjacent values at powers of ten, and a deterministic 10,000
iteration xorshift64 stream seeded with `0x123456789abcdef0`.

The upstream formatter is used only to generate the reference data. The app
uses Rust's Ryu digits with the Swift formatting rules; it does not link Swift.
Reference source URLs and SHA-256 checksums:

- [SwiftDtoa.cpp](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift/swift-6.2-RELEASE/stdlib/public/runtime/SwiftDtoa.cpp):
  `1cdf7d33001fd05a5f98f63b78fe4c7140176c69f3615f293e484b1c4d5f3e41`
- [SwiftDtoa.h](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift/swift-6.2-RELEASE/include/swift/Runtime/SwiftDtoa.h):
  `4016b34b10353bf9da2165aa7060fe703b2c2413e8c53a8d8ea9980958527041`

Compile the upstream C source with binary64 support enabled and the other
formats disabled. The original corpus harness is in
[`../reference/swift-double.c`](../reference/swift-double.c); its tab-separated
output is the fixture. The source downloads retain their upstream Apache-2.0
with Runtime Library Exception license and are not vendored into the app.

`sync-wire-v1.json` was generated with that same independent Swift formatter
and OpenSSL-backed HKDF/AES-GCM. It has a different sync root (`0x99 × 32`) and
salt (`0xaa × 32`) from the vault fixture. It supplies both the exact canonical
plaintext/hash and the encrypted `snippets-wire-v1` records, including a secure
record whose inner vault ciphertext is preserved verbatim. It also supplies
independent SHA-256 membership/dataset digests with UInt32 big-endian length
framing. No Rust serializer, crypto implementation or digest helper was called
to produce these reference bytes.

These tests demonstrate byte and cryptographic compatibility against the
reference generators. They do not replace an end-to-end run between the Linux,
Swift and Android applications, or a real account's server integration test.

`merge-v1.json` contains independent conflict-snapshot SHA-256, UUIDv5 and
effective-deletion-set fingerprints generated with Python's standard library.
Its simple binary64 dates have the same exact canonical spelling in Swift.
No Rust merge, encoder, UUID or digest helper produced these expected values.
